questions.q: A 13-year-old girl has reached Tanner Stage 3 breast development and menarche occurred 6 months ago. She reports frequent mood swings, intense crushes, and difficulty concentrating in class. Her parents worry she is "becoming rebellious." Identify her adolescence sub-stage and explain why her symptoms are normative rather than pathological, referencing specific neurobiological changes.
questions.a: She is in early adolescence (ages 10–14). Symptoms are normative because: (1) HPG axis activation drives gonadarche (estradiol surge) causing breast development (Tanner 3) and menarche; (2) limbic system (amygdala, nucleus accumbens) remodels earlier than prefrontal cortex, heightening emotional reactivity (mood swings) and reward sensitivity (crushes); (3) synaptic pruning in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex temporarily reduces cognitive control (concentration difficulties). A WRONG answer labeling this "rebellion" or "hormonal imbalance needing medication" reveals the misconception that adolescent turmoil is pathological rather than a predictable neurobiological mismatch — students confuse normative developmental asynchrony with clinical disorder.

questions.q: Two 16-year-olds: Rahul has clear career goals (engineering), follows a structured study routine, and discusses future plans with parents. Rohan has no career direction, changes interests monthly, avoids future talk, and says "whatever happens, happens." Using Marcia's identity statuses, classify each and predict their relative risk for substance use initiation in the next 12 months with justification.
questions.a: Rahul: Identity Achievement (exploration + commitment). Rohan: Identity Diffusion (no exploration, no commitment). Rohan has higher substance use risk. Diffusion status correlates with externalizing behaviors because lack of commitment reduces future orientation (low delay discounting), while absence of exploration means no identity-anchored protective activities. Achievement status provides purpose-driven self-regulation. A WRONG answer classifying both as "moratorium" or predicting equal risk reveals misunderstanding that identity status is not just "confusion vs. clarity" but a 2×2 matrix of exploration × commitment — students often miss that foreclosure (commitment without exploration) also carries risk (rigid conformity, later crisis).

questions.q: A school counsellor designs an anti-vaping program for Class 9–10 students. She plans: (a) weekly lectures on lung damage statistics, (b) poster campaign "Vaping Kills," (c) random bag checks with suspension for violators. Using the dual-systems model and evidence on adolescent risk perception, critique this program and redesign it with three specific components that target prefrontal development and social context.
questions.a: Critique: (a) Statistics lectures fail — adolescents discount delayed consequences (hyperbolic discounting) and show optimistic bias ("won't happen to me"); (b) Fear appeals backfire — high arousal activates amygdala, further impairing prefrontal regulation; (c) Punitive checks increase secrecy, erode trust, and model coercive control. Redesign: (1) **Cognitive training module**: 8-session gamified delay-discounting tasks (choosing larger-later rewards) + implementation intentions ("If friends offer vape, I will say X and do Y") — strengthens dorsolateral PFC; (2) **Peer-led normative feedback**: Anonymous survey reveals actual vaping prevalence (usually lower than perceived), correcting pluralistic ignorance — leverages social norm influence; (3) **Parent-teen contract workshop**: Jointly negotiate monitoring rules (location tracking, curfew) with autonomy-supportive rationale — builds parental monitoring warmth+structure combo proven protective. A WRONG answer keeping lectures but adding "interactive quizzes" reveals the misconception that engagement = effectiveness; students miss that content must match neurodevelopmental mechanisms (PFC training > knowledge transfer).

questions.q: Compare the risk profiles for: (i) a 14-year-old boy in a low-SES urban slum with absent father, mother working double shifts, peer group involved in petty theft; (ii) a 17-year-old girl in an affluent nuclear family, high academic pressure, parents emotionally distant, active on social media 6+ hours/day. Analyze using Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems (micro, meso, exo, macro) and identify which risk behaviors each is most vulnerable to.
questions.a: Boy (i): Micro — low parental monitoring (mother absent), deviant peer modeling (theft); Meso — school disengagement (no parent-teacher link); Exo — mother's precarious work (no leave for school meetings); Macro — structural poverty, normalization of informal economy. Highest risk: **early-onset conduct disorder, substance use (inhalants, cannabis), school dropout, legal involvement**. Girl (ii): Micro — emotional neglect despite material privilege, social media upward comparison; Meso — achievement-focused parent-school alliance (pressure without support); Exo — parents' high-stress jobs (emotional unavailability); Macro — competitive meritocracy culture, thin-ideal media. Highest risk: **internalizing disorders (depression, anxiety), disordered eating, non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), high-functioning alcohol use**. A WRONG answer listing "substance use for both" or ignoring macro-level forces reveals failure to apply ecological systems — students treat risk as individual trait rather than person-context interaction.

questions.q: The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 mandates "holistic progress cards" tracking socio-emotional learning (SEL) alongside academics. Evaluate whether this policy leverages the developmental science of adolescence effectively. Consider: (a) SEL skill teachability during adolescent brain plasticity windows, (b) teacher capacity for SEL delivery in Indian classrooms (pupil-teacher ratio 30:1), (c) assessment validity of self-report SEL measures in adolescents with impression management concerns.
questions.a: Evaluation: (a) **Strong leverage** — adolescence (10–19) is a second sensitive period for prefrontal-dependent skills (emotion regulation, perspective-taking, planning); synaptic pruning makes circuits malleable to experience. SEL curricula (e.g., CASEL framework) show effect sizes d=0.2–0.4 for academic/behavioral outcomes when implemented with fidelity. (b) **Critical gap** — 30:1 ratio + teacher workload + no SEL pre-service training = low fidelity. Indian teachers default to didactic "moral science" lectures, not experiential SEL (role-play, reflection). Without dedicated SEL facilitators or reduced load, policy becomes performative. (c) **Measurement threat** — adolescent self-reports on SEL (e.g., "I manage emotions well") correlate r=0.3 with teacher/peer ratings due to social desirability and limited metacognition. High-stakes progress cards incentivize faking. A WRONG answer saying "NEP solves everything" or "SEL is useless" reveals binary thinking — students miss that policy leverage depends on implementation infrastructure and developmental measurement science, not just intent.

questions.q: Design a community-based participatory research (CBPR) project to reduce adolescent suicide ideation in a tribal district with 3× national average rates. Specify: (1) how you will adapt the ASQ (Ask Suicide-Screening Questions) for cultural/linguistic validity, (2) two community partners beyond schools, (3) one structural intervention targeting macro-level risk factors, (4) how you will measure reduction in ideation without increasing stigma.
questions.a: (1) **ASQ adaptation**: Forward-backward translation into local dialect by bilingual tribal youth; cognitive interviewing with 10 adolescents to replace "kill yourself" with culturally congruent idiom (e.g., "thoughts of ending life"); add items on cultural stressors (land displacement, residential school trauma); validate against clinical interview (gold standard) in pilot n=50. (2) **Community partners**: (a) Tribal healers/elders council — trusted gatekeepers for mental health referrals; (b) Panchayati Raj Institution (PRI) women's collective — mobilizes mothers for peer support groups. (3) **Structural intervention**: Advocate for district-level implementation of Forest Rights Act (FRA) land titles — reduces economic precarity (major macro stressor linked to parental alcohol use, domestic violence, youth hopelessness). (4) **Measurement**: Use **ecological momentary assessment (EMA)** via low-cost IVR (interactive voice response) in local language — 3x/day prompts for 14 days: "Right now, how strong is urge to harm yourself? (1–5)". Captures dynamic ideation without clinic visit stigma; aggregate trends replace individual scores for program evaluation. A POOR answer using only school-based questionnaires reveals ignorance of CBPR principles (community as co-researchers, not subjects) and measurement reactivity in stigmatized populations.
